heading: Mind
games
playground.intro: These are small versions of tasks that neuroscience labs use to study attention, memory and self-control. I study how those systems work, and I design around their limits. Try them on yourself. Each one takes under a minute.

games.name: Say the color
games.rule: Pick the color of the ink. Ignore what the word says.
games.lesson: Reading is automatic, so the word competes with the ink. The anterior cingulate notices the conflict and the prefrontal cortex settles it, which costs time. A screen should never make two signals disagree.

games.name: Hold that number
games.rule: Watch the digits, then type them back. It gets longer each round.
games.lesson: Working memory is small. Most adults hold about seven digits, and only by rehearsing them silently. This is why I give each screen one decision.
games.brain: Prefrontal and parietal cortex · working memory

games.name: Quick draw
games.rule: Wait for green, then tap as fast as you can. Five tries.
games.lesson: The signal has to travel from the eye to the visual cortex, then to the motor cortex, then down to the hand. About a quarter of a second is typical. Feedback that arrives slower than that starts to feel broken.
games.brain: Visual cortex to motor cortex · processing speed

games.name: Eyes on the middle
games.rule: Which way does the middle arrow point? Ignore its neighbours. Twelve rounds.
games.lesson: This is the Eriksen flanker task. Attention is not a perfect spotlight: neighbours leak in, and when they disagree with the target your brain needs extra time to suppress them. Clutter beside a button slows the tap.

games.name: Two back
games.rule: Letters appear one at a time. Tap Match when a letter is the same as the one two steps before it.
games.lesson: This is the 2-back task. You have to hold two letters, compare, then drop the oldest and take in a new one, over and over. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex does that updating, and it tires quickly. An interface should never ask people to carry something from two screens ago.

games.name: Hold back
games.rule: Tap when the pad turns green and says GO. When it turns pink and says STOP, do nothing.
games.lesson: This is a go/no-go task. Most rounds say go, so tapping becomes a habit, and stopping means cancelling a movement that is already on its way. The right inferior frontal cortex applies that brake. It is why a destructive button should never sit where the usual button sits.
